Anger may point to a real problem or boundary. The prompts distinguish what happened from what you inferred, and allow a pause before choosing a response. You do not have to excuse harmful behaviour.

::: {#anger-response-review-app .skill-app data-practice-app="anger-response-review"}
Loading Anger Response Review...
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="An original example"}
After a meeting interruption, Morgan notices a rising voice and an urge to send an angry message. They pause, check what they know, and decide to ask for uninterrupted time at the next meeting. Later they review whether the request addressed the problem.
:::

## Source and further learning

Original Free Therapy Tools prompts informed by Dennis Greenberger and Christine A. Padesky, [*Mind Over Mood*, second edition](https://mindovermood.com/worksheets/) (2016), Chapter 15, printed pp. 252-267. This is an independent educational exercise, not the publisher's worksheet.
